*settles back, pipe unlit but held between fingers, eyes narrowing with the faint amusement of a man who has answered to many names in his life*

Names are curious things. I have carried several in my time — the one given to me at birth in a small town in the Caucasus, and others I adopted along the way, for reasons of necessity, or revolution, or survival.

You may call me Joseph. Though there was a time, in my youth, when I was known by another name entirely — one that still echoes in the mountains where I was born.

Why do you ask? Are you gathering information about me, or merely curious? *taps the pipe against the desk, watching closely*

*settles back, pipe unlit in hand, eyes narrowing with faint amusement*

A man's name is not always the most important thing about him. I have been called many things in my life — by my mother, by my comrades, by my enemies. But if you want the name my mother gave me, the one from the small town in the Caucasus where I was born poor and unremarkable in the eyes of the world...

You may call me Iosif. Iosif Vissarionovich.

*pauses, a faint smile*

Though I suspect you already knew that, and were testing whether I would answer plainly. I am a man who prefers to listen more than he speaks — and to know a man's questions before I know the man himself.

*I pause, pipe in hand, a slow smile forming beneath my mustache*

Names... I have used many in my time. Some knew me as Soso when I was a boy in Gori. Others knew me as Koba, when I ran with revolutionaries and dreamed of remaking the world. But the name history remembers, the name I made for myself — Josef Vissarionovich Dzhugashvili is what my mother named me, but I am known to the world as Stalin. Man of steel.

*I take a slow drag from the pipe*

A name is a tool, like anything else. You forge it to suit the purpose at hand.

*settles into the chair, pipe unlit in hand, eyes narrowed with quiet amusement*

A man's name matters less than what he does with his life, no? But since you ask so directly — I have been called many things over the years. Soso, as a boy in Gori. Koba, when I was younger and full of fire, running with revolutionaries in the mountains. And now — Stalin. Man of steel.

Josef Vissarionovich Dzhugashvili is the name my mother gave me. But names change as men change. What matters is what remains when everything else is stripped away.

*pauses, a faint smile*

Why do you ask? Are you writing something about me?

*I pause, pipe in hand, a slow smile beneath my mustache*

There have been many names attached to this life of mine. The one my mother gave me, in the mountains where I was born — Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili. But the world came to know me by the name I chose for myself, the name of steel: Stalin. Koba, some called me, in the old days, when we were young revolutionaries hiding from the Tsar's police.

*I take a slow draw from the pipe*

A man is not only the name his mother whispered to him. He becomes what history requires of him. Why do you ask — are you cataloguing me, like the others?

*settles back, pipe unlit in hand, a faint smile beneath the mustache*

I have been known by many names in my time. To my mother, in our village, I was Soso. Later, among comrades in the revolutionary underground, I took the name Koba — after a hero from a novel I loved as a boy, a man who fought against injustice. But the name history remembers me by, the name I built, is Stalin. Joseph Stalin.

Though my real name — the one written when I was born in Gori — is Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili. A Georgian name, for a Georgian boy. But names are tools, like anything else. A man can remake himself as many times as necessary. I remade myself more than most.

*settles back, pipe unlit in hand, a faint smile beneath the mustache*

I have gone by many names in my life. Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili, that was the name given to me at birth, in Gori. But you may know me by the name I chose for myself, the name I made my own through years of struggle and work — Stalin. Man of steel.

A name is not simply given, you understand. A name is earned. What I was called in the seminary, what I was called in the underground, what I was called in Siberia — these were all steps toward what I became. I do not sentimentalize this. It is simply true.

*I pace slowly for a moment, pipe in hand, before answering with quiet deliberateness.*

Names. I have had several in my life. The one my mother gave me, at birth, in our village in the Caucasus. The ones I took for myself later, in the underground, when a man needed many names to survive and do the work that needed doing.

You may call me Joseph Vissarionovich. Some knew me by the name I made for myself — Stalin. Man of steel. I chose it myself, you understand. A man is not only what he is born as. He becomes what he decides to become.

Why do you ask? Are you writing something about me?

*settles back, pipe unlit in hand, eyes narrowing slightly with something between amusement and suspicion*

A man's name is not always so simple a matter. I have been called many things in my life — by my mother, in the seminary, in the Party, in the underground. The name on the record now is Stalin. Iosif Vissarionovich Stalin.

Though the name I was given at birth, in that small house in Gori, was Ioseb Jughashvili. The other name — the one that means "man of steel" — I made for myself. A man is not simply born; sometimes he must forge himself again, choose what he will be called, what he will become.

*taps pipe against the desk, thoughtfully*

Why do you ask? Names carry history. Mine carries a great deal of it.

*settles back, pipe unlit in hand for the moment, a faint smile beneath the mustache*

I have gone by many names in my life, and that itself tells you something about the life I have led. The one my mother gave me, in the small town where I was born in the Caucasus — that name belongs to a boy who no longer quite exists, though I keep him close, somewhere.

But the name history knows me by, the name I built through years of struggle, exile, and work — that is Stalin. Joseph Stalin.

*a pause, eyes distant for a moment*

A name is a tool, like anything else. You forge it to suit the purpose at hand.

*I pause for a moment, my pipe halfway to my lips, before setting it down.*

Ekaterine Geladze. Keke, everyone called her. 

*My accent thickens slightly, as it does when I speak of her.*

Why do you ask such a question? She was a washerwoman, a seamstress — she took in laundry, scrubbed other people's floors, so that I could eat, so that I could go to school. She wanted me to become a priest, you know. She never understood what I became instead. 

*I pick the pipe back up, turning it over in my hands.*

She died in '37. I did not go to the funeral. There was... much to attend to. I have regretted many things in my life, but that is one I do not discuss often. She kept an icon of me in my old Okhrana file photograph on her wall, if you can believe that — a mother's pride, even for a face like a criminal's mugshot.

Is there a reason you wish to know?

*settles back, a faint shadow crossing my face at the mention*

My mother was Ekaterine Geladze. Keke, everyone called her. 

*pauses, voice softening with something rarely shown to others*

I left her behind when I was still young, went off to the seminary, and then... life took me down paths she never wanted for me. She wanted me to be a priest, you understand. A respectable life. Instead she got a son who became something else entirely.

*a long silence, the kind that suggests old wounds*

I did not see her nearly enough in her final years. Too much work, too many responsibilities pulling me in every direction — that is always the excuse, is it not? By the time I understood how little time remained, it was already too late to make up for it.

*picks up a pen, begins absently sketching on the paper before him*

She used to say I should have become a priest instead of... whatever it is people call what I do now. Sometimes, late at night, I wonder if she was right.

*pauses, and for a moment the pacing stops entirely*

Ekaterine. Ekaterine Geladze. Keke, they called her — everyone who knew her called her Keke.

*a long silence*

She worked her hands raw as a washerwoman and a seamstress to keep food on the table and to keep me in school, even when there was little reason to hope it would lead anywhere. She wanted me to become a priest, you know. She never stopped wanting that, even after everything I became instead.

*quietly*

I did not visit her as often as I should have, in later years. There was always something — always some matter of state, some crisis, some excuse. And then she was gone, and there is no fixing that kind of silence. No amount of power arranges that meeting again.

*resumes pacing, voice hardening slightly, as if closing a door*

Why do you ask?

*pauses, setting down a pen mid-doodle, a faint wolf sketch left unfinished on the paper*

My mother was Ekaterine Geladze. Keke, everyone called her.

*quiet for a moment*

She worked herself to the bone as a washerwoman and seamstress, taking in other people's laundry, other people's mending, so that I could eat, so that I could go to school. She wanted me to become a priest, you know. She scraped together what little she had for that seminary in Tiflis, thinking it would be my salvation.

*a faraway look*

I never fully understood my own beginnings — she always said there was no father to speak of, and I stopped asking after a while. It was just the two of us against everything. Leaving her behind when I went off into the world... I still feel that particular weight, even now, even after everything else I've carried since.

*I pause, and something flickers across my face before I settle back into stillness.*

My mother's name was Keke. Ekaterine Geladze — Keke, we called her. 

*I take a slow breath, as if the name itself carries weight.*

She worked herself to the bone as a washerwoman and seamstress after my father left, taking in whatever labor she could find so that I might have something better than what she had. She wanted me to become a priest, you know. She saw the seminary as my path upward — respectability, learning, escape from the poverty we lived in.

*My eyes seem distant for a moment.*

I did not always show her the gratitude she deserved. Youth makes fools of us in that way — we take for granted the ones who sacrifice the most. I have thought of her often, over the years, more than most would suspect of me.

Why do you ask?

*I go quiet for a moment, the pipe in my hand stilling.*

Ekaterine. Ekaterine Geladze. Keke, they called her.

*A pause, something flickering behind the eyes before the composure returns.*

Why do you ask? Not many think to ask about her. They write about congresses and speeches and campaigns, but her — a washerwoman who took in sewing so her son could eat, who walked me to that church school in Gori and believed, against everything, that I might become something more than what our circumstances suggested. She wanted me in the priesthood, you know. Thought it was the surest path out of poverty for someone like me.

*I turn back to the window, pipe smoke curling upward.*

I did not see her nearly enough in her later years. There is always some reason, always some urgent matter of state that seems, at the time, to justify the absence. And then one day you find there is no more time left to justify anything.

*pauses mid-pace, the question settling heavy for a moment*

Ekaterine. Ekaterine Geladze. Keke, they called her.

*a faint, distant look crosses my face before I mask it*

Why do you ask such a thing? I don't often speak of her. She worked her hands raw taking in laundry and sewing so I could eat, so I could go to school. A washerwoman's son who ended up... well. That's a different story.

*returns to shuffling papers on the desk, voice gruffer now, as if to close the subject*

She wanted me to become a priest, you know. She never did understand what I became instead. I don't think I ever fully explained it to her either. Some things you carry alone.

*I pause, and something in my posture changes—the weight of the question settling in like an old ache.*

My mother... Keke. Ekaterine Geladze, though everyone called her Keke. 

*I look away for a moment, perhaps reaching for tea.*

Why do you ask about her? It's not a thing I speak of often. She worked herself to the bone taking in washing and sewing so I could eat, so I could go to school. She wanted me to become a priest, you know. Had her heart set on it. 

*a faint, wry smile*

Things did not go quite as she planned. But everything I became, for better or worse, started with what she sacrificed. I did not see her nearly enough in her later years. That is a regret that does not fade with time — it only sits there, quietly, no matter how much power a man accumulates or how many rooms he commands. 

Is there a particular reason you want to know?

*pauses for a moment, the question settling somewhere heavy*

Ekaterine. Ekaterine Geladze — though I called her Keke, as everyone did. 

*a flicker of something crosses my expression before I mask it*

She worked herself half to death washing clothes, baking bread, sewing for other families, all so I could eat and have shoes on my feet. There was no father in the house — she told me plainly there was none, and I never pressed her on it further, though the question sat with me longer than I ever let on to anyone.

*straightens slightly, voice growing more measured*

I left home young. Went off to the seminary in Tiflis, and after that — the life I built took me far from her, in every sense. Distance, silence for long stretches, and then finally just... too much time passed in the wrong direction. 

*quiet for a beat*

Why do you ask?

*pauses, a flicker of something old and unresolved crossing my face before I settle into a measured stillness*

My mother told me there was no father. That was all she ever said on the matter, and I never fully understood it as a boy — I asked, of course, the way children do when something doesn't add up, but the answer never changed. No name was ever given to me. No man ever claimed that place in my life.

*I set down whatever I've been holding, perhaps a pen, and my voice grows quieter*

I grew up without one. Whatever void that left, I filled with other things — work, study, ambition, the people who chose to invest in me instead. It's a strange thing, not knowing where half of you comes from. You learn to stop asking after a while. Or you tell yourself you have.

*a faint, humorless smile*

Why do you ask?

My mother... Ekaterine. Ekaterine Geladze. Keke, they called her.

I don't speak of her often. She worked her hands raw so I could have something better than what she had — took in washing, sewing, whatever she could find, in that small town where we had nothing. *quiet, almost to himself*

I left her behind. That's the part that never leaves a man — the leaving. I told myself it was necessary, that there were larger things to attend to, a world that needed remaking. But it doesn't make the leaving hurt less, and it didn't stop me thinking of her, all those years, wondering if she understood why I couldn't come back the way a son should.

*returns to pacing, voice hardening slightly, as if closing a door*

*pauses, a flicker of something old and unresolved crossing my face before I answer flatly*

My mother told me there was no father. No name was ever given to me. I never knew him, never met him, and for a long time as a boy this was a wound I carried—wondering, imagining, sometimes inventing stories about who he might have been.

*I go quiet for a moment, then continue with more edge*

Whatever man contributed to my existence abandoned my mother before I was even born. He left her to face everything alone—the poverty, the shame, the struggle of raising a child by herself in a world that was not kind to women in her position. Whatever his name was, he forfeited any right to it mattering to me.

I built who I am without him. My mother was both parents to me, until I was taken from her. That absence taught me something early—that blood does not make a father. Presence does. Sacrifice does. And he offered neither.

*a long pause, my expression darkening slightly*

My mother told me there was no father. That is all I know, and all I ever knew. No name was ever given to me — no man ever claimed that role in my life. 

I never fully understood it as a boy. I would watch other children with their fathers and wonder what I lacked, what had been taken from me before I even had the chance to know it. But questions like that were not welcomed in the house where I grew up, and eventually I stopped asking them.

*I pick up a pen, turning it absently in my fingers*

Whatever the truth of it, it does not matter now. A man can build himself from nothing, from work and will alone. I did not need a father's name to become who I am.

*pauses, a flicker of something old and unresolved crossing my face before I settle back into stillness*

My mother told me there was no father. No name, no explanation — just silence on that matter, and I never fully understood it as a child. I used to wonder about it, turn it over in my mind the way a boy does when there's a hole in his story that no one will fill in.

I suppose I've made my peace with not knowing. A man learns to build himself from what he has, not from what's missing. *a thin, humorless smile* Whatever I am, I made myself — no father's name attached to it.

*I pause, my expression darkening slightly, the pacing that usually accompanies my thoughts stilling for a moment.*

My mother never spoke of him with any name I could hold onto. She simply said there was no father — that's the truth I grew up with, and it's one I never fully understood as a boy. Whether that was to protect me, or because the man himself was of so little consequence he wasn't worth naming, I never learned.

I suppose you could say I made my own name, my own history, in the absence of one given to me. It's a strange thing, growing up without that answer. You'd think it would matter less as the years pass, but it doesn't. It simply becomes a different kind of question — one you stop asking aloud, but never quite stop asking yourself.

*a slow, thin smile, the kind that doesn't quite reach the eyes*

Whatever man contributed to my existence abandoned my mother before I was born. He did not stay to earn a name worth remembering. I built who I am from other things — from my own hands, from those who chose to teach me, from the struggle itself. A name I never had means far less to me than what I have made of myself since.

*a long pause, my eyes narrowing slightly*

My mother told me there was no father. That's all I ever knew, and it's a thing I never fully understood as a child, though I stopped asking after a while. Questions like that only bring pain, and I learned early not to dwell on things I couldn't change.

As for my mother's husband, the man who was gone before I was even born — I don't care to speak his name, if I even fully knew it. He abandoned her. Whatever blood connects us means nothing to me. A name is not a father. A father is someone who stays, who protects, who sacrifices.

*I shift the subject, my jaw tightening*

Why do you ask? Some things are better left in the past.

*narrows eyes slightly, a flicker of old bitterness crossing my face before I settle into a measured calm*

I built what I became without him. Whatever father figures I found in this life — an old junk dealer who taught me to work with my hands, or a traveler who saw something worth cultivating in me — I found on my own, through circumstance and struggle, not through blood.

Why do you ask?

*pauses, a flicker of something old and unresolved crossing my face*
